characters: Adwoa: an eleven-year-old Ghanaian girl in Primary 6, bright eyes, natural hair tied in two neat puffs with purple ribbons, wearing a yellow polo shirt, denim overalls and carrying a small spanner and sketchbook.
Kojo: Adwoa’s ten-year-old brother, supportive and cheerful, wearing a green t-shirt and khaki shorts.
Papa Kwame: Adwoa and Kojo’s father, a warm carpenter and devoted dad in his thirties, wearing a blue shirt (and a clean patterned apron when cooking supper).
Mama Esi: Adwoa and Kojo’s mother, an agricultural extension officer in her thirties, wearing a purple-and-gold wax-print top.
Auntie Serwaa: a visiting mechanical engineer in her thirties, wearing a smartteal work shirt and safety glasses.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, spirited Ghanaian storyteller (en-GH); bright and determined for Adwoa, cheerful for Kojo, warm and wise for Papa Kwame, Mama Esi and Auntie Serwaa.
notes: Pronounce Adwoa ("ah-JOH-ah"), Kojo ("KOH-joh"), Kwame ("KWAH-meh"), Esi ("EH-see") and Serwaa ("sehr-WAAH") clearly.

music: Optional joyful highlife guitar and light percussion; off by default.
culturalNotes: Celebrates both Ghanaian women engineers and men who proudly share caregiving and cooking at home.
reviewQuestions: Does the story model mutual respect between girls and boys and shared family responsibility without blaming any group?

pages.brief: Sunny Ghanaian courtyard: Adwoa (11, hair in two puffs with purple ribbons, yellow shirt, denim overalls, holding a sketchbook and small spanner) watching farm cooperative members shell bowls of dried groundnuts by hand.
pages.narration: Warm, observant opening introducing Adwoa’s love for machines and the real-world problem she spots.

pages.brief: By the compound gate: Adwoa holding her small spanner and gear sketch looking momentarily hurt as a passing male neighbour gestures dismissively.
pages.narration: Show the restrictive stereotype clearly without caricature.

pages.brief: Warm family veranda scene: Papa Kwame (wearing a clean patterned apron over his blue shirt, holding a wooden ladle) smiling proudly with Mama Esi (holding a tablet) and brother Kojo (hanging clothes on a line).
pages.narration: Warm, dignified scene showing shared household and caregiving responsibilities in action.

pages.brief: Around the veranda workbench: Papa Kwame and Mama Esi smiling encouragingly at Adwoa while brother Kojo hands her a bicycle sprocket.
pages.narration: Heartfelt, positive affirmation of equal capability and shared family teamwork.

pages.brief: At the workbench: Auntie Serwaa (teal work shirt, safety glasses on head) pointing to Adwoa’s drawing of a bicycle chain connected to a cylindrical drum and mesh sieve (no text).
pages.narration: Clear, exciting STEM mentorship from Auntie Serwaa.

pages.brief: Workshop table: Adwoa using a metal ruler to measure the narrow gap between a wooden roller and a wire mesh screen inside an open wooden hopper, while Kojo and Auntie Serwaa watch closely.
pages.narration: Show real engineering problem-solving: measuring clearance and adjusting force.

pages.brief: Close view of the pedal-powered machine: Adwoa tightening a bolt with her spanner as clean red groundnut kernels drop into a steel bowl underneath and papery shells blow into a basket on the side.
pages.narration: Step-by-step physics and mechanical design: friction cracks the shell, gravity drops the dense kernel, airflow separates the light husk.

pages.brief: In the courtyard: Kojo holding a stopwatch while Adwoa points to a mechanical dial scale holding a full bowl of clean groundnut kernels beside the pedal sheller (no numbers on the scale).
pages.narration: Clear, verifiable arithmetic: 5 kg in 10 minutes × 6 = 30 kg per hour (6 times faster than 5 kg/hour by hand).

pages.brief: Lively outdoor school science fair under a canopy (no text banners): Adwoa pointing confidently to the chainring and drum while Kojo pedals and a crowd of farmers, students and teachers watch in admiration.
pages.narration: Proud, collaborative presentation by Adwoa and Kojo.

pages.brief: At the fair table: the older male neighbour shaking Adwoa’s hand with genuine respect and warmth while Papa Kwame, Mama Esi, Auntie Serwaa and Kojo smile proudly.
pages.narration: Gracious, restorative moment showing how excellence and respect change minds.

pages.brief: Warm family living room at night: Adwoa and Mama Esi sketching machine gears at the table while through the open kitchen doorway Papa Kwame and Kojo cheerfully dry plates together.
pages.narration: Warm, inspiring conclusion celebrating equal opportunity and shared family partnership.

teacherGuide.overview: An uplifting Primary 5–JHS 1 story combining simple machines (wheel-and-axle, gear ratios, winnowing airflow) and rate arithmetic (5 kg per 10 minutes = 30 kg/hour) with a warm, constructive portrayal of gender equality in STEM and shared family caregiving.
learningGoals: Explain how simple machines (pedals, chain-and-sprocket gears, rollers, winnowing fans) reduce human drudgery in agriculture.
Calculate hourly production rates from 10-minute test data (5 kg × 6 = 30 kg/hour vs 5 kg/hour by hand).
Recognise that engineering, leadership, cooking and caregiving abilities are not limited by gender.
Practise respectful collaboration between girls and boys at school and at home.

beforeReading: Preview the title and cover illustration with learners and ask what real-world problem or question the characters might face.
whileReading: Pause at the embedded comprehension and vocabulary activities to check understanding and discuss the evidence in the text.
afterReading: Gear-Ratio Tooth Count: On a bicycle, count the teeth on the front chainring (e.g., 44 teeth) and the rear sprocket (e.g., 22 teeth) to see why one turn of the pedals turns the back wheel twice.
Density & Winnowing Demo: Drop small pebbles and tiny torn bits of dry leaf in front of a hand fan to observe how airflow pushes light husks sideways while heavier seeds fall straight down.
discussion: Why did Papa Kwame say "a spanner does not ask whether the hand holding it belongs to a girl or a boy, and neither does a cooking pot"?
How did Kojo and Adwoa work as true partners rather than competitors?
What physical difference between groundnut kernels and dry shells allows the fan to separate them (winnowing)?
How did the neighbour react when he saw the evidence of Adwoa’s working machine at the fair?
reflection: How did the neighbour react when he saw the evidence of Adwoa’s working machine at the fair?

whatWeKnow: Mechanical threshers and shellers use controlled shear clearance (slightly larger than the seed kernel, smaller than the outer pod) plus aerodynamic winnowing to separate grain from chaff.
Educational research across Ghana and globally confirms that girls and boys have equal aptitude for mathematics, science and engineering when given equal encouragement and practice.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Agricultural engineers in Ghana are designing solar- and pedal-powered multi-crop shellers with interchangeable screens for groundnuts, maize and cowpeas.

investigation.title: Airflow Winnowing Separation Test
materials: A tray, 20 dried beans or small pebbles, 20 tiny pieces of dry paper or dry leaf husks, and a piece of stiff card to fan gently.
steps: Mix the 20 dried beans and 20 tiny paper husks together in a small cup.
Pour the mixture slowly from a height of 20 cm onto the tray while a partner waves the stiff card gently from the side to create a light breeze.
Observe where the heavy beans land compared with where the light paper husks blow!

pronunciation.guidance: "ah-JWAH". The "dw" is the hard part for English engines and is probably not a plain "d" + "w".
reviewerNotes: HIGH RISK: the "dw" cluster. Native speaker to demonstrate and approve a rendering.

pronunciation.guidance: "KWAH-meh". English speakers often say "KWAH-mee"; confirm the final vowel.
reviewerNotes: Confirm final vowel (meh vs mee) and the "kw" onset.
